evidence_quotes.quote: The goal is to protect water from source to tap to minimize risk so that people have access to adequate and safe drinking water. The federal government has committed to assist First Nations achieve comparable levels of service standards available to non-First Nation communities.

However, their capacity or flexibility to plan and design a drinking water treatment plant is limited because of the AANDC formula for determining the appropriate level of service standards for a community. Under this arrangement, the federal government has the dual role of funding and enforcement agent.
Non-First Nations are able to charge for services and generate tax revenue, which is more sustainable, whereas, First Nations must rely on conditional federal funding.
Through the Access to Information Act the federal risk evaluation surveys of First Nations drinking water systems in Ontario were obtained for 2005 and 2007.

A survey based on the federal risk evaluation guidelines was sent to municipalities and townships throughout Ontario. A total of 54 municipalities and townships throughout the province completed it (Figure 2).

In many First Nations, the service standards to ensure adequate and clean drinking water are not being met. According to the federal Risk Evaluation (Figure 5a), the drinking water systems in 83 First Nations were at medium or high risk, while only 12 were reported to supply a sufficient volume of water to the community.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community-level drinking water service standards and capacity to provide adequate and safe drinking water across First Nation reserve communities and non-First Nation municipalities in Ontario, including system capacity to meet demand and sufficiency of water volume supplied to communities.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain reading: Yes — extensively examines legal, regulatory, institutional, and governance arrangements for First Nation versus municipal drinking water systems in Ontario (Ontario statutory regime under Safe Drinking Water Act / O. Reg. 170/03, Clean Water Act, and Sustainable Water and Sewage Systems Act versus the federal non-statutory policy/guideline gap, Indian Act s. 81(1)(l), Bill S-11/S-8, and fragmented federal agency oversight). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes (borderline) — compares community water systems across two distinct utility regulatory, financing/cost-recovery, and enforcement structures governing community service standards and capacity: non-First Nation municipal utilities under binding provincial statutory regulation with municipal user-fee and tax cost-recovery powers versus First Nation Band-administered systems governed by AANDC service-standard funding formulas, conditional 80/20 O&M cost-sharing rules, compliance enforcement via funding holdbacks or third-party management, and a Band Council Resolution / by-law opt-in requirement to participate in provincial Clean Water Act source water protection committees. It is somewhat borderline because the quantitative comparison aggregates these rule-type differences at the First Nation versus municipal system level and centers primarily on a multi-barrier water-safety risk index rather than isolating individual rules at the household connection level, so both plain_criterion2_decision and decision are include (with medium confidence).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary and administrative empirical evidence: compares 2005 and 2007 federal AANDC Risk Level Evaluation assessments for 143 First Nation drinking water systems in Ontario (obtained via the Access to Information Act) against a primary survey of 54 Ontario municipalities and townships using the equivalent risk evaluation instrument.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports community/system-level outcomes relevant to service availability, reliability, quantity, and safe drinking water standards: overall and domain-specific risk rankings (source water, design capacity/reliability, operation, reporting, operator), whether systems supply a sufficient volume of water to the community (12 of 143 First Nation systems reported yes, with 128 missing), whether systems are at capacity struggling to meet demand, occasional water shortages, boil water advisories, and Drinking Water Quality Guideline / coliform exceedances.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (143 First Nation community drinking water systems and 54 municipal/township drinking water systems in Ontario), exposure (First Nation federal non-statutory/conditional-funding regulatory regime vs. Ontario provincial municipal statutory/cost-recovery regulatory regime), outcome (multi-barrier drinking water system risk scores and component service capacity/volume/quality indicators), and study design (cross-sectional comparative administrative and survey study) are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Cross-sectional comparative observational study combining federal administrative risk evaluation records (2005 and 2007) and a primary municipal survey
population_and_sample: Community drinking water systems in Ontario, Canada: 143 First Nation drinking water systems across 137 First Nation communities and 54 non-First Nation municipal and township drinking water systems (unit of analysis: community drinking water system)
exposure: Regulatory, institutional, and financing regime governing community drinking water systems: First Nation on-reserve regime (federal policy directives without statutory drinking water standards, AANDC service-standard funding formulas, conditional 80/20 operating cost-sharing, enforcement via withholding project funds or third-party management, and by-law/Band Council Resolution opt-in requirement for provincial source water protection) versus non-First Nation municipal regime (binding Ontario statutory drinking water and source water protection regulations with municipal fee and tax cost-recovery authority)
outcome: Federal Drinking Water Risk Evaluation rankings (low, medium, high risk on a 1-10 scale) across source water, design (including treatment capacity to meet demand and system reliability), operation (including supplying a sufficient volume of water to the community, bacteriological compliance, and boil water advisories), reporting, operator qualifications, and overall system risk, plus source water protection plan adoption and occasional water shortages
rationale: Full text matches record R70B810197AA2 (Walters et al., 2012). The study empirically compares 143 First Nation community drinking water systems in Ontario (using 2005/2007 federal AANDC Risk Level Evaluation data obtained via Access to Information Act) against 54 non-First Nation municipal/township systems surveyed with the same instrument. It satisfies C1 and C4 at the community/utility level because, alongside water-quality safety, the risk evaluation and reported findings examine community drinking water service standards, treatment capacity to meet demand, operational reliability, occasional water shortages, and whether systems supply a sufficient volume of water to the community. It satisfies C2 under both the plain wording and (as a borderline community/system-level case) the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading by comparing utilities operating under two distinct regulatory, financing/cost-recovery, and enforcement structures in Ontario: municipal systems under binding provincial statutes and fee/tax cost recovery versus First Nation systems governed by non-statutory federal protocols, AANDC service-standard funding formulas, conditional 80/20 O&M cost-sharing, funding-withholding enforcement, and by-law opt-in conditions for provincial source water protection. Confidence is medium because the empirical analysis compares the two regimes at the aggregate First Nation vs. municipal group level and centers primarily on a multi-barrier drinking-water risk index rather than household-level access connections.
